title: Moby-Dick
objective: After this level you can explain how Melville turned a whaling voyage into an epic of obsession.
summary: Melville turned his whaling years and the wreck of the Essex into Moby-Dick (1851): Captain Ahab's revenge hunt for the white whale, an epic novel that flopped and was rediscovered in the 1920s.

cards.headline: "Call me Ishmael." Then a whaling voyage turns into something much bigger.
cards.body: Herman Melville knew whaling firsthand. In January 1841, at 21, he sailed out of New Bedford harbor on the whaleship Acushnet. His narrator, Ishmael, later calls a whale ship "my Yale College and my Harvard". Moby-Dick (1851) starts out as a sailor's story. It doesn't stay one.

cards.headline: One captain, one passion
cards.body: The Pequod's captain, Ahab, has lost a leg to a white whale called Moby Dick. He tells his crew plainly: "it was Moby Dick that dismasted me". From then on the voyage bends toward a single target. Ishmael says Ahab "seemed ready to sacrifice all mortal interests to that one passion". A business trip for whale oil has become a revenge quest, and the whole crew is aboard for it.

cards.headline: An epic, in prose
cards.body: Level 1 drew the line: an epic is a long narrative poem of heroic deeds, while a novel is an invented story in prose. Moby-Dick is a novel, yet it is often called Melville's "epic novel", and it has the scale: a towering captain, a doomed quest, an ocean-sized stage. Hawthorne is widely credited with inspiring Melville to turn early drafts of a sea adventure into this huge book, and Melville dedicated it to him.

mascot.line: People mix these up. An epic is a poem. Moby-Dick borrows the epic's size, but in prose, so it is still a novel.

cards.context: In the final chase Ahab cries "from hell's heart I stab at thee", the whale destroys the Pequod, and only Ishmael survives to tell it. Real life supplied the shape: in 1820 a sperm whale rammed and sank the whaleship Essex, a story Melville first heard aboard the Acushnet. Moby-Dick flopped with critics and buyers and was not rediscovered until the 1920s.

learned: Melville sailed on the whaler Acushnet
Ahab's one passion: revenge on the white whale
An epic novel: epic scale in prose
The Essex wreck shaped the ending

questions.prompt: Why is Captain Ahab hunting Moby Dick?

options.label: The whale took his leg, and he wants revenge
Its oil would make him rich
options.rationale: Ahab cares about one whale, not profit.

options.label: He wants to study it for science

questions.explanation: Moby Dick "dismasted" Ahab, taking his leg, and Ahab sacrifices everything to that one passion.

questions.prompt: How did real events feed into Moby-Dick?

options.label: Melville interviewed a real Captain Ahab
It retells a Greek epic line by line
Melville never went to sea and worked from dreams
Melville sailed on a whaler and heard of the Essex

questions.explanation: Melville sailed on the Acushnet in 1841 and there heard of the Essex, sunk by a sperm whale in 1820.

questions.prompt: By Level 1's definitions, why is Moby-Dick a novel rather than a true epic, despite its epic scale?

options.label: It is an invented story in prose, not a poem
It has no central character at all
It is too short to count as an epic
It was composed aloud by singers

questions.explanation: An epic is a long narrative poem; a novel is an invented prose story. Moby-Dick borrows epic scale in prose.
